title: Command-line arguments: argc and argv
learningObjectives: Explain the topic and its C rules.
Trace the example and explain its data or control flow.
Identify edge cases and resource-management requirements.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: A hosted C program may receive command-line arguments through main's argc and argv parameters. argc counts the argument strings, and argv points to an array of pointers to null-terminated strings; argv[argc] is a null pointer.
understand.whyItMatters: Command-line arguments make programs scriptable and allow users to configure input paths and options without interactive prompts.
understand.analogy: Treat each algorithm or resource as a contract whose invariants must remain true after every operation.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal rules for pointers, object lifetime, complexity or library contracts.

explain.narrative:
A hosted C program may receive command-line arguments through main's argc and argv parameters. argc counts the argument strings, and argv points to an array of pointers to null-terminated strings; argv[argc] is a null pointer.

State preconditions, invariants, empty and full cases, ownership and failure behaviour before implementation. Compile with warnings and test normal, boundary and failure paths.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The loop visits each argument string from index zero through argc minus one. The first argument is conventionally the program name, though its exact content is implementation-defined.

practise.guidedTask: Predict argc and argv entries for a command with two user-supplied arguments.
practise.independentTask: Add an option parser that validates a numeric argument and handles missing or extra arguments.
hints: Check argc before accessing argv at a particular index.
Treat command-line text as untrusted input and validate conversions.
Do not assume argv[0] contains an absolute path.
